new_statements.quote: [Kato 2022: 28] As shown in Table 1, there are four tones: low-level, high-level, falling, and checked tones. [...] Additionally, there are atonic syllables, and they are represented by not adding any tone marks. The only rhyme that can appear in atonic syllables is /-ə/. These are pronounced short and weak. [Kato 1995: 73, Kyonbyaw dialect] The only vowel that can occur in an atonic syllable is /ɤ/. Atonic syllables are represented as /Cɤ/. They never occur in utterance final position. When they are followed by a word boundary (or morpheme boundary), they are represented as /Cɤ-/ so as to denote that they cannot occur singly.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. (1) Kato 2022, lines 173-177 (text layer of; page footer '― 28 ―' follows the checked-tone paragraph, so the passage is on p. 28, sec. 2 'Phonology of Western Pwo Karen'): 'As shown in Table 1, there are four tones: low-level, high-level, falling, and checked tones.... Additionally, there are atonic syllables, and they are represented by not adding any tone marks. The only rhyme that can appear in atonic syllables is /-ə/. These are pronounced short and weak.' Verbatim; the elided sentences are about the tone marks on /a/ and [ä]. Table 1 lists à [a11], á [a55], â [a51], aʔ [aʔ51], ə atonic exactly as reported. (2) Kato 1995, lines 466-470 = sealang scan page 11; I rendered tha…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Western Pwo Karen (Kyonpyaw/Pathein) is a lexical tone language: every full syllable bears one of four tones (low-level 11, high-level 55, falling 51, checked ʔ51). The only non-tonal syllables are 'atonic' Cə (1995: Cɤ) minor syllables, which are short and weak, contain only schwa, never stand utterance-finally or alone, and lean on a following tonic syllable (sesquisyllabic CəCV́ words, e.g. /pəlôuʔ/ 'shirt'). No word-stress/accent rule is stated for full-syllable sequences.
new_statements.exceptions: Some disyllables alternate between tones (numerals lose low tone to falling before classifiers; 'one' /lɤ̀/ > proclitic /kɤ-/ before a classifier); checked vs falling tone confusable for some speakers. No stress exceptions since no stress rule is given.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern syllable types within the (phonological) word and utterance: atonic syllables barred utterance-finally and cannot occur singly; described from elicited citation forms and texts (Kyonpyaw dialect, fieldwork 1993-95 and later).
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand descriptions (Kato 1995 sec. 1; Kato 2022 sec. 2) describe the dialect of Kyonpyaw (Kyonbyaw) town, Pathein District, Ayeyarwady Region, which Kato states is 'not substantially different' phonologically from the Pathein (Bassein) dialect described by Jones 1961; this is squarely Glottolog pwow1235 / ISO pwo. CAUTION: Glottolog's ref 'Phillips 2000, West-Central Thailand Pwo Karen Phonology' (listed under pwow1235) actually describes WCT Pwo Karen of Sisawat, Kanchanaburi, Thailand, an Eastern-type Pwo variety (Ethnologue puts WCT Pwo under ISO kjp = pwoe1235); its explicit 'Stress and rhythm' section therefore does NOT belong to pwow1235. Duffin 1913 and Purser & Tun Aung 1922 are identified by Kato (2013: 99-100) as Western (delta) Pwo Karen.

sources.locator: Kato 2022 sec. 2 'Phonology of Western Pwo Karen', p. 28 (Table 1); Kato 1995 sec. 1.6 'Atonic Syllables', p. 73
sources.note: Sec. 2 (pp. 27-30), Kyonpyaw dialect: syllable C1(C2)V1(V2)(C3)/(T); four tones (low-level 11, high-level 55, falling 51, checked ʔ51) plus atonic syllables whose only rhyme is /-ə/, 'pronounced short and weak', written without tone mark. No word-stress rule; the word 'stress' is not used.

sources.citation: Phillips, Audra. 2000. West-Central Thailand Pwo Karen phonology. 33rd ICSTLL, Bangkok: Ramkhamhaeng University, 99-110.
sources.note: Sec. 3 'Stress and rhythm' (pp. 99-100): words show either an unstressed-stressed iambic pattern (minor+major) or, in major+major words, stress on the first major syllable (/mɤ'mi/ 'sun'?); destressed proclitics attributed to phrase-level rhythm. BUT this is WCT Pwo Karen of Kanchanaburi, Thailand (Eastern-type), not pwow1235.

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 1995. The phonological systems of three Pwo Karen dialects. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 18.1: 63-103.
sources.note: Sec. 1 Kyonbyaw (Western) dialect: three tonemes (high-level, low-level, falling; falling realised [53] before final ʔ); sec. 1.6 Atonic syllables: only vowel /ɤ/, never utterance-final, 'cannot occur singly' (written /Cɤ-/). 'Stress' appears only in the Hpa-an (Eastern) section ('unstressed form /lɤ-/' of 'one').

sources.note: Eastern Pwo (Hpa-an) phonology: atonic /-ə/ syllables 'pronounced short and weak'. Background only (not Western Pwo).

sources.note: For Eastern Pwo: atonal syllables 'phonetically unstressed and short', sesquisyllabic words = 'unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable'; 'In PK and SK, the minor syllable in a sesquisyllabic word never has a tone'. Family-level, not specific to Western Pwo.
